unit-alg-0104.title: Topic 1 · 1-4 Arithmetic Sequences and Series
unit-alg-0104.srcName: enVision Algebra 2, Lesson 1-4 Arithmetic Sequences and Series (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 1-4 from the enVision Algebra 2 student edition: arithmetic sequences and the sums of their terms. Covers the common difference, recursive and explicit definitions and translating between them, solving problems with a sequence, the formula for the sum of a finite arithmetic series and where it comes from, sigma notation, and finding how many terms a series has.

why.text: A sequence is just a function whose inputs are 1, 2, 3, so everything from the first three lessons still applies — this is where that pays off. The explicit formula is what lets you jump straight to the 100th term, and the sum formula turns adding fifty numbers into one multiplication.

objectives.text: Decide whether a sequence is arithmetic and find its common difference
Write both recursive and explicit definitions, and convert between them
Use the explicit formula to find any term, or to find d from two known terms
Find the sum of a finite arithmetic series
Read and evaluate a sum written in sigma notation
Find the number of terms when a series is given up to its last value

parentNote.text: Built from the 1-4 student edition. No answer keys had been uploaded for this lesson when I built it (1-1, 1-2 and 1-3 all have them), so every answer here is derived independently and checked by a second method where one exists — the log-stack answer, for instance, is verified against the n(n+1)/2 result. If the keys appear later I will re-check against them. The two reliable stumbling blocks are both off-by-one errors: (n − 1) rather than n in the explicit formula, and counting terms inclusively when a series runs from a named start to a named end (June to December is 7 months, not 6). Both get their own card and a question.

nextUp.text: The formulas are short but the off-by-one errors are relentless. Check every answer at n = 1 before moving on.

cards.def:
**A function whose domain is the natural numbers — an ordered list of terms.**
• The input is the term NUMBER; the output is the term itself.
• Writing it as a function is what lets you use everything you already know about functions on it.

**A sequence with a constant difference between consecutive terms.**
• 3, 8, 13, 18, 23 adds 5 every time, so it is arithmetic.
• 1, 4, 9, 16 is not — the gaps are 3, 5, 7, which are not constant.
cards.hint: Subtract each term from the next. If you get the same number every time, it is arithmetic.

cards.def:
**The constant amount added to get from one term to the next, written d.**
• Find it by subtracting any term from the one after it.
• d can be negative, which just means the sequence is going down. 97, 86, 75 has d = −11.

**Defines each term using the previous one, plus a stated starting value.**
• aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + d for n > 1, together with a₁.
• The starting value is not optional — without it there is nothing to build from.
cards.hint: Recursive means "in terms of itself". You must be told where to start.

cards.def:
**Gives any term directly from its term number, with no need for the previous term.**
• aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1).
• Use this when you want the 100th term and have no interest in the 99 before it.

**Because the first term has had NO common differences added yet.**
• The 1st term has 0 differences added, the 2nd has 1, the 3rd has 2.
• So term n has (n − 1) of them — always one fewer than the term number.
cards.hint: Off by one, every time, and for a reason: you start AT the first term, you do not step to it.

cards.def:
**Read a₁ and d off the recursive rule and drop them into aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1).**
• Given a₁ = 3 and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 0.5, the explicit form is aₙ = 3 + 0.5(n − 1).
• Nothing is computed — the two definitions carry the same two numbers.

**The number multiplying (n − 1) is d, and substituting n = 1 gives a₁.**
• For aₙ = 16 − 3(n − 1): d = −3, and a₁ = 16 − 3(0) = 16.
• So the recursive form is a₁ = 16, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ − 3 for n > 1.

cards.term: Two forms of the same explicit rule
cards.def:
**aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1) can always be expanded into the form aₙ = dn + c.**
• For −1, 6, 13: a₁ = −1 and d = 7, so aₙ = −1 + 7(n − 1).
• Expanding: −1 + 7n − 7 = 7n − 8. Both are correct and give identical terms.
• If two people disagree about the formula, test both on n = 1 and n = 2 rather than arguing.

**The SUM of the terms of a sequence.**
• A sequence is the list; a series is what you get when you add the list up.
• A finite series adds a fixed number of terms.
cards.hint: Sequence, list. Series, sum. Both start with s, which is exactly why they get confused.

cards.term: Sum of a finite arithmetic series
cards.def:
**Multiply the number of terms by the average of the first and last, which is what the formula does.**
• Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ) / 2.
• You need three things: n, the first term and the LAST term. If the last term is missing, find it first.

cards.term: Where the sum formula comes from
cards.def:
**Write the series forwards, write it backwards underneath, and add the two.**
• Every column then sums to a₁ + aₙ, and there are n columns.
• That double-counts the series, so 2Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ) and you halve it.
• Worth knowing because it means you can rebuild the formula if you forget it.

**A compact way to write a sum: the index counts from the bottom number to the top one.**
• The expression to the right of Σ is the rule for each term.
• Σ from i = 1 to 12 of (7i − 5) means add up 7i − 5 for i = 1, 2, 3, … , 12.

cards.term: Finding n from the last term
cards.def:
**When a series is written out to its final value, solve aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1) for n.**
• For 2 + 9 + 16 + … + 79: a₁ = 2, d = 7, aₙ = 79.
• 79 = 2 + 7(n − 1) gives 77 = 7(n − 1), so n − 1 = 11 and n = 12.
• You cannot use the sum formula until you know how many terms there are.

questions.q: What makes a sequence arithmetic?
opts: There is a constant difference between consecutive terms
There is a constant ratio between consecutive terms
Every term is a whole number
The terms always increase
questions.hint: Test it by subtracting neighbours, not dividing them.
steps: Subtract each term from the one after it.
If every one of those differences is the same number, the sequence is arithmetic.
A constant RATIO would make it geometric instead, which is a different kind of sequence.

ex.main: **A constant difference between consecutive terms.** That constant is d, the common difference.
ex.tip: Arithmetic goes with adding. A sequence built by multiplying is geometric.

questions.q: What is the common difference of 40, 33, 26, 19, …?
questions.hint: Subtract a term from the one that follows it, keeping the order right.
steps: Take the second term minus the first: 33 − 40 = −7.
Check with the next pair: 26 − 33 = −7. Same.
So d = −7. The sequence is decreasing, which is what a negative d means.

ex.main: **−7.** The sign matters — dropping it would send every later term the wrong way.
ex.tip: Always subtract in the order "later minus earlier". Reversing it flips the sign.

questions.q: What does a recursive definition of a sequence need in order to work?
opts: A starting value
The last term
The sum of all the terms
At least ten terms
questions.hint: A recursive rule tells you how to get the next term from the previous one. What is missing at the very beginning?
steps: A recursive rule says how to get each term from the one before it.
At the first term there is no previous term to use.
So the definition must state a₁ outright, or the chain never gets started.

ex.main: **A starting value.** The book lists leaving it out as the common error, and it makes the definition genuinely useless.
ex.tip: Recursion always needs a base case. That is true here and in every other place recursion shows up.

questions.q: What is the difference between a sequence and a series?
opts: A sequence is the list of terms; a series is their sum
A sequence is finite; a series is infinite
A sequence uses addition; a series uses multiplication
They are two words for the same thing
questions.hint: One of them is a single number at the end.
steps: A sequence is an ordered list: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13.
A series is what you get by adding that list: 1 + 4 + 7 + 10 + 13.
The sequence has five terms; the series has one value, 35.

ex.main: **A sequence is the list; a series is the sum.** The two words look alike and mean genuinely different things.
ex.tip: If the answer is a list, it is a sequence. If the answer is one number, it is a series.

questions.q: Which formula gives the sum of a finite arithmetic series?
opts: Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ) / 2
Sₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1)
Sₙ = n · d
Sₙ = (a₁ + aₙ) / n
questions.hint: The sum needs the number of terms, the first term and the last term.
steps: aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1) gives a single term, not a sum, so that one is out.
The sum formula multiplies the number of terms by the average of the first and last.
The average of the first and last is (a₁ + aₙ) / 2.
So Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ) / 2.

ex.main: **Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ) / 2.** Read it as "how many terms, times the average term".
ex.tip: That reading makes it memorable: for an arithmetic sequence, the average of the first and last IS the average of the whole list.

questions.q: In the explicit formula aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1), why is it (n − 1) and not n?
opts: The first term has had no common differences added to it yet
Because sequences start counting at zero
To make the formula work for negative d
It is a convention with no reason
questions.hint: Count how many times you add d to get from the 1st term to the 3rd.
steps: To reach the 1st term you add d zero times — you are already there.
To reach the 2nd you add d once; to reach the 3rd, twice.
So reaching the nth term takes (n − 1) additions, always one fewer than the term number.
That is exactly what (n − 1) counts.

ex.main: **The first term has had no common differences added yet.** The off-by-one is doing real work, not decoration.
ex.tip: Check any sequence formula at n = 1. If it does not return a₁, something is wrong.

questions.q: Is 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 an arithmetic sequence?
opts: No — the differences are 2, 4, 8, 16, which are not constant
Yes, with d = 2
Yes, with d = 4
Yes, because every term is even
questions.hint: Work out all the differences before deciding, not just the first one.
steps: Differences: 4 − 2 = 2, then 8 − 4 = 4, then 16 − 8 = 8, then 32 − 16 = 16.
Those differences are 2, 4, 8, 16 — not the same number each time.
So the sequence is not arithmetic. It is geometric, since each term is double the previous.

ex.main: **No.** The first difference being 2 is a trap; you have to check them all before calling a sequence arithmetic.
ex.tip: Always compute at least three differences. One pair proves nothing.

questions.q: Write the explicit definition for the sequence 11, 18, 25, 32, …
questions.hint: Identify a₁ and d, then substitute into aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1).
steps: The first term is a₁ = 11.
The common difference is 18 − 11 = 7, and 25 − 18 = 7 confirms it.
Substitute into aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1): aₙ = 11 + 7(n − 1).
Check at n = 1: 11 + 7(0) = 11. Correct.

ex.main: **aₙ = 11 + 7(n − 1).** Testing n = 1 immediately rules out aₙ = 11 + 7n, which would give 18.
ex.tip: You could also expand it to aₙ = 7n + 4. Both are right; check them at n = 1 and n = 2 to be sure.

questions.q: Given aₙ = 9 + 4(n − 1), what is the recursive definition?
opts: a₁ = 9, and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 4 for n > 1
a₁ = 4, and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 9 for n > 1
a₁ = 13, and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 4 for n > 1
a₁ = 9, and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 9 for n > 1
questions.hint: The number multiplying (n − 1) is d. Substitute n = 1 to get the first term.
steps: The coefficient of (n − 1) is 4, so d = 4.
Substitute n = 1: a₁ = 9 + 4(1 − 1) = 9 + 0 = 9.
A recursive definition needs both the start and the step.
So: a₁ = 9, and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 4 for n > 1.

ex.main: **a₁ = 9, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 4.** The two forms hold the same two facts; only the packaging changes.
ex.tip: Answer 13 comes from mistakenly computing 9 + 4(1). Always substitute into (n − 1), not n.

questions.q: An auditorium has 20 seats in the first row and 32 seats in the fifth row, increasing arithmetically. How many seats are in the tenth row?
questions.hint: Use the two known rows to find d first, then apply the explicit formula to row 10.
steps: Use aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1) with a₁ = 20, n = 5 and a₅ = 32.
Then 12 = 4d, giving d = 3.

ex.main: **47 seats.** Two known terms are always enough to pin down d, and then any term is one substitution away.
ex.tip: Note 5 − 1 = 4, not 5. The off-by-one is where this question is won or lost.

questions.q: What is the sum of the arithmetic series with 12 terms, a₁ = 5 and a₁₂ = 60?
questions.hint: You have all three pieces the sum formula needs. Substitute carefully.
steps: Use Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ) / 2.
Substitute: S₁₂ = 12(5 + 60) / 2.
Inside the bracket: 5 + 60 = 65.

ex.main: **390.** Forgetting to halve gives 780, which is the most common wrong answer here.
ex.tip: Sanity-check it: the average term is 32.5, and 12 × 32.5 = 390. Consistent.

questions.hint: Count the terms, then use the first and last with the sum formula.
steps: Count the terms: 4, 9, 14, 19, 24, 29, 34 — that is n = 7.
First term a₁ = 4, last term a₇ = 34.

ex.main: **133.** With only seven terms you could add them directly — and doing so is a good way to check the formula.

questions.q: What is the sum of the series written in sigma notation as Σ from i = 1 to 8 of (3i + 2)?
questions.hint: Find the first and last terms by substituting i = 1 and i = 8, then use the sum formula.
steps: There are n = 8 terms, counting from i = 1 to 8.

ex.main: **124.** Sigma notation is only a compact way of writing the series — find the ends and the ordinary formula applies.
ex.tip: You never have to expand a sigma sum term by term. First term, last term, how many. That is all it needs.

questions.q: How many terms are in the series 6 + 13 + 20 + … + 90?
questions.hint: Use the explicit formula with the last term known and solve for n.
steps: First term a₁ = 6, and d = 13 − 6 = 7.
The last term is 90, so 90 = 6 + 7(n − 1).
Subtract 6: 84 = 7(n − 1).
Divide by 7: 12 = n − 1, so n = 13.

ex.main: **13 terms.** Stopping at n − 1 = 12 and answering 12 is the standard slip — remember to add the 1 back.
ex.tip: Check it: a₁₃ = 6 + 7(12) = 6 + 84 = 90. Correct.

questions.q: Two students write formulas for −1, 6, 13, 20, …. One writes aₙ = −1 + 7(n − 1); the other writes aₙ = 7n − 8. Who is right?
opts: Both — expanding the first gives the second
Only the first
Only the second
Neither
questions.hint: Expand the first formula and compare, then test both at n = 1.
steps: Expand the first: −1 + 7(n − 1) = −1 + 7n − 7 = 7n − 8.
That is exactly the second formula, so they are the same rule written differently.
Test both at n = 1: the first gives −1 + 0 = −1; the second gives 7 − 8 = −1. Both correct.
Test at n = 3: first gives −1 + 14 = 13; second gives 21 − 8 = 13. Both correct again.

ex.main: **Both.** aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1) always expands into the form dn + c, and neither version is more correct.
ex.tip: When two formulas look different, expand one or test both on a couple of terms. Do not argue from appearance.

questions.q: A stack of logs has 12 logs on the bottom row and one fewer in each row above, ending with 1 log at the top. How many logs are in the stack?
questions.hint: This is a series. Identify n, a₁ and aₙ before reaching for the formula.
steps: The rows hold 12, 11, 10, … down to 1, so this is arithmetic with d = −1.
There are 12 rows, so n = 12, with a₁ = 12 and a₁₂ = 1.

ex.main: **78 logs.** Whether you count from the top or the bottom does not matter — the first and last terms just swap places, and their sum is unchanged.
ex.tip: This is the classic 1 + 2 + … + n sum, which always comes to n(n + 1) / 2. Here 12 × 13 / 2 = 78.

questions.q: A saver deposits $30 in June and increases each monthly deposit by $4, finishing in December. How much has been saved in total?
questions.hint: Count the months carefully first — that is where this one is usually lost.
steps: June to December inclusive is 7 months: June, July, August, September, October, November, December.
So n = 7, with a₁ = 30 and d = 4.
The last deposit is a₇ = 30 + 4(7 − 1) = 30 + 24 = $54.

ex.main: **$294.** Counting the months inclusively is the real difficulty — 7 months, not 6, because June itself counts.
ex.tip: Whenever a problem names a start and end point, count them out. December minus June is 6, but the answer is 7.

questions.q: Why does writing an arithmetic series forwards and backwards, then adding, give the sum formula?
opts: Every column then adds to a₁ + aₙ, and there are n columns, giving twice the sum
Because addition is commutative, so the order does not matter
Because the middle term is always the average
Because the common difference cancels out of every term
questions.hint: Line up 1 + 4 + 7 + 10 + 13 above 13 + 10 + 7 + 4 + 1 and add each column.
steps: Write the series forwards and again backwards, lined up in columns.
In each column, moving right in one row adds d while moving right in the other subtracts d, so every column has the same total.
That total is the first plus the last: a₁ + aₙ. With n columns, the two rows together come to n(a₁ + aₙ).
But the two rows are the series counted twice, so 2Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ), and Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ) / 2.

ex.main: **Every column adds to a₁ + aₙ, and there are n of them.** Knowing this means you can rebuild the formula if it slips your mind in an exam.
ex.tip: Commutativity is why you are allowed to reverse the order, but it is the constant column sum that produces the formula.

questions.q: A colony has 175 bees in week 1 and grows arithmetically to 259 by week 4. In which week does it first exceed 1,015 bees?
opts: Week 31
Week 30
Week 32
Week 29
questions.hint: Find d from the two known weeks, then solve for the n that reaches 1,015.
steps: From week 1 to week 4 is 3 steps: 259 = 175 + d(4 − 1), so 84 = 3d and d = 28.
Divide by 28: 30 = n − 1, so n = 31 — the colony reaches exactly 1,015 in week 31.

ex.main: **Week 31.** The population hits 1,015 exactly then, so that is the first week it is not below the limit.
ex.tip: Check: a₃₁ = 175 + 28(30) = 175 + 840 = 1,015. Exact, which is why the wording matters.

questions.q: A student claims 0, 1, 3, 6, 10, … is arithmetic with a next term of 15. What is right and what is wrong?
opts: The next term is 15, but the sequence is not arithmetic — the differences grow
The sequence is arithmetic, but the next term is 14
Both claims are correct
Both claims are wrong
questions.hint: Check the differences, then check whether the pattern still predicts a next term.
steps: Those are 1, 2, 3, 4 — increasing, not constant, so the sequence is NOT arithmetic.
But the pattern is still clear: the next difference is 5, giving 10 + 5 = 15.
So the predicted term is right and the classification is wrong.

ex.main: **The next term is 15, but the sequence is not arithmetic.** These are the triangular numbers; their differences are arithmetic, the sequence itself is not.
ex.tip: A predictable pattern is not the same as an arithmetic one. Arithmetic demands a CONSTANT difference.
